passage:
Varun and Rehana raced to the door when Papa's scooter buzzed, elbows out. Rehana touched the handle first. "I win!" Varun's chest burned. He had wanted so much to be first. Papa said, "You both ran so fast!", hugged them each, and promised each of them a story time of their own that week.

That afternoon Rehana tore Varun's drawing of a giraffe in half while grabbing the crayons. Varun's whole body went hot and he smacked her arm. She wailed. Amma came. "You hit, so no crayons for now. But what could you say instead?" Varun sniffled. "You broke my giraffe, I am mad." He had not said that before. Amma put a strip of tape across the drawing.

When both had stopped crying, Rehana pushed her stuffed rabbit into his hands. "Sorry. Here." Varun's shoulders dropped, and he felt light again. He gave her the tape to hold.

On Monday in the school yard, a bigger boy began tugging at Varun's bag. Rehana marched over and stood right beside her brother, chin up, then ran to Salma Miss. "That boy is bothering Varun." The teacher came at once.

qa.q: What did Rehana hand Varun to say sorry?
qa.a: She handed him her stuffed rabbit.

qa.q: How did the two children treat each other at home when they raced and fought, compared with the school yard?
qa.a: At home the race and the torn drawing left them hurt, crushed and hitting. In the school yard the fights did not matter: Rehana stood right beside Varun and fetched Salma Miss.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when Rehana touched the door handle first?
qa.a: He felt crushed and jealous. His chest burned because he had wanted so much to be first.

qa.q: What could Varun say and do instead of hitting when a drawing is torn?
qa.a: He could say, "You broke my giraffe, I am mad," and get help from Amma, as he did.

grounding: Two young siblings race for Papa's attention, fight over a drawing, repair it with a toy and a sorry, and then stand together against a bigger child.

passage:
Gargi sat on her bed at night, sure she had no gift of any kind. Manjula could sing like a bird, and her cousin Nikhil won every quiz. At dinner Papa said, "Look at your cousin Nikhil, he plays the flute so well." Gargi's chest crumpled and she put down her spoon. "I do try, just differently from him," she said. "Can you notice something I did today?" Papa paused. "You fed the neighbour's cat every day this week."

At school Manjula sang the morning song and the whole hall went still. Gargi's mouth fell open. Instead of deciding she could never, she asked after class, "How do you practise?" Manjula grinned. "Every morning, with my grandmother's harmonium." She sang the tune again slowly so Gargi could try.

Over the term Gargi tried drums, chess and clay. She was slow at chess, dropped the drums, and loved clay. In March she took a small clay owl to the district fair and won a prize. The applause made her cheeks glow. Afterwards she thanked Aditi Ma'am, who had taught her to knead, and stayed behind to show two younger children how to roll a coil.

qa.q: What did Gargi make that won a prize?
qa.a: She made a small clay owl.

qa.q: How did Gargi's reaction to Manjula's singing differ from her reaction to Papa's comparison, and what changed by March?
qa.a: Papa's comparison crushed her, though she spoke up for herself. Manjula's singing amazed her, and she asked how to practise instead of giving up. By March, after trying drums, chess and clay, she loved clay and won a prize.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when Papa praised Nikhil's flute playing?
qa.a: She felt crushed. Her chest crumpled and she put down her spoon.

qa.q: How did Gargi stay humble after winning the prize?
qa.a: She thanked Aditi Ma'am, who had taught her to knead, and stayed behind to show two younger children how to roll a coil.

grounding: A child who feels she has no special talent is compared with a cousin, admires a classmate's singing, tries several things and wins a prize she shares humbly.

passage:
The Thursday satsang felt like family to Elizabeth, who had moved to the city alone. Someone always saved her a cushion, and she was welcome even on days she doubted a verse. She kept her Sunday football and her old friends.

Darshan, her neighbour, was deeper in. He handed over his savings, then his weekends, cooking for two hundred without pay. His friend Imran worried. Imran did not say the teacher was a fraud. He asked, "What do you love about it?" and "What if you wanted a break?" Darshan looked away. Imran still came every Saturday with samosas, and kept saying, "My door is open."

Then the teacher asked Elizabeth for a large donation and told her not to mention it to her family. Her stomach dropped. She rang her brother. "It is not foolish of you," he said. "Step back and talk to someone outside." Weeks later, a former volunteer showed her proof that the teacher, who preached having little, owned three flats and had buried a complaint about a member being mistreated. Elizabeth felt grief and anger. She helped the volunteer take the complaint to the proper authority. She kept the breathing practice she had learned, and did not decide that every sincere person was fake.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask of Elizabeth?
qa.a: The teacher asked for a large donation and told her not to mention it to her family.

qa.q: How did Imran's way of handling Darshan's commitment differ from Elizabeth's response when the teacher made demands?
qa.a: Imran stayed warm, asked open questions and kept his door open without attacking the teacher, so Darshan could still turn to him. Elizabeth, faced with a secret donation demand, stepped back, talked to her brother, and later helped take a buried complaint to the proper authority.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she learned about the teacher's flats and the buried complaint?
qa.a: She felt grief and anger, after having found family in the satsang.

qa.q: Why did Imran keep visiting Darshan every Saturday?
qa.a: Keeping the friendship alive means Darshan can turn to him when doubts rise.

grounding: Belonging in a satsang, a friend's total giving that worries a caring friend, secret demands for money, and a teacher's hidden wrongdoing show the pressures of one community.

passage:
A message popped up in Nirmala's game chat: "Hi, you play really well!" from a name she did not know. It seemed interesting, and she wanted to reply. She took the tablet to her mother, Bhavna, instead. "Not yet," said Bhavna. "Let me look. We never share our school, address or photos." They blocked the account together.

Two weeks later, Madhav's face at recess was grey. A stranger from his game had asked for photos, and lately wrote that they knew where Madhav lived. Madhav had frozen, kept the messages and stopped answering, but he was too ashamed to tell his parents, sure they would be angry that he had chatted at all.

Nirmala saw the screen over his shoulder. "That's scary. You have to tell someone." "No! Promise you won't," he hissed. Nirmala's stomach hurt. She did not want him angry with her, but his safety mattered more than the secret. That afternoon she told her mother. Bhavna hugged her, said she had done the right thing, and phoned Madhav's mother straight away. Madhav's parents came over that evening. Madhav showed them the saved messages, cried, and heard, "You are not in trouble. We are on your side." They took the messages to the school and to the helpline that same night.

qa.q: What did the stranger ask Madhav for?
qa.a: The stranger asked Madhav for photos.

qa.q: How did Nirmala's first meeting with a stranger's message differ from Madhav's, and what did Nirmala's telling do?
qa.a: Nirmala took the message to her mother before replying, and they blocked the account together. Madhav kept his chat secret out of shame until the stranger frightened him. Nirmala told her mother despite his anger, and the adults helped him that same day.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he begged Nirmala not to tell?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid his parents would be angry that he had chatted at all.

qa.q: What did Madhav do right after the stranger said they knew where he lived?
qa.a: He froze, kept the messages and stopped answering.

grounding: One child's curious message is checked with a parent, while a friend's secret chat with a stranger who threatens him becomes a same-day matter for adults because the first child tells.

passage:
Rashmi's Sunday began at her faith community's kitchen, washing steel plates beside Ritu, feeling held by a group who had brought soup when her father was in hospital last year. Her thanks that morning was quiet: for his long recovery, for the neighbour who had driven them, for the people who had paid what they owed on time. She let it show in small ways. She slipped a bag of rice into Ritu's cart for the food drive and said nothing about it.

Later a new group leader spoke at the gathering. "Give three months of your salary, and do not question what we teach." Rashmi's mind pricked. She loved the chanting and the service, and she did not love that. She said calmly, "I would like to see how the funds are used, and I have questions about the rule." The room went quiet.

Noor, who followed no religion and sat at the back, thanked her afterwards for asking. Rashmi invited Noor to tea, and the next week to the harvest meal with the community. They swapped stories with open curiosity.

qa.q: What did Rashmi slip into Ritu's cart?
qa.a: She slipped a bag of rice into it.

qa.q: How did Rashmi's gratitude and sense of belonging differ from her response to the leader's demand?
qa.a: Her gratitude turned into small generous acts, and her community's warmth felt like being held. When the leader demanded three months of salary and no questions, she kept the chanting and service but asked how the funds were used, and stayed open to Noor.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when the leader said not to question what they teach?
qa.a: She felt uneasy. Her mind pricked, though she loved the chanting and the service.

qa.q: How did Rashmi show openness to people outside her community?
qa.a: She invited Noor to tea and then to the harvest meal with the community, and they swapped stories with open curiosity.

grounding: A woman's devotion combines belonging in a faith community, quiet gratitude turned into generosity, and calm questions to a leader who demands money and obedience.

passage:
On Monday, Bhupen presented the new tracker layout to the team as if he had drawn it up himself. Avni had sketched it in a chat on Thursday. Her face went hot and her jaw tightened, and she felt used. She nearly stood up and said so in front of everyone. Instead she stayed silent through the meeting.

That afternoon she collected the chat messages and the dated drafts. She asked Bhupen for five minutes. "That layout came from my Thursday message. Next time, can we say whose idea it was?" Bhupen shifted. "I built on it." "You did, and I want it to be clear." She began sending her updates in writing to the whole team, and at the start of any project she said what each person owned. If it happened again, she decided, she would take the dated messages to the manager as plain facts.

Amandeep, seated beside her, seethed in another way. When Bhupen's promotion was announced a month later, Amandeep felt bitter and had nothing kind to say in the pantry. Then Avni said, "Show your work. Post your fixes in the weekly notes." Amandeep began writing a Friday summary of what had been done and by whom. By the next review, the manager was quoting it.

qa.q: When had Avni sketched the tracker layout?
qa.a: She had sketched it in a chat on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Avni's handling of the credit-taking differ from Amandeep's reaction to Bhupen's promotion?
qa.a: Avni collected the messages and dated drafts and raised it calmly, then began sending written updates so everyone saw who did what. Amandeep first felt bitter after the promotion, then started a Friday summary that made the work visible.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling in the Monday meeting?
qa.a: She felt angry and used. Her face went hot and her jaw tightened.

qa.q: What could Avni do if it happened again?
qa.a: She could take the dated messages and drafts to the manager as plain facts.

grounding: One colleague presents another's work as their own, which brings anger and betrayal to the one wronged and bitterness to a bystander who then learns to make work visible.
